title: How agencies lose the second project
metaTitle: Why the second project never starts
excerpt: The next engagement dies when launch ends in a zip file and the people who knew the decisions leave. Leave a system, and a way back to the same team.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, a kept arrangement for an article about work that has to remain findable after launch.
caption: A wall that stays legible after the meeting ends. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why do studios lose the project after launch?
faqs.answer: The usual cause is a handoff that is only a folder of files, plus a team change. The client cannot find the decision, so they either freeze or hire someone who will redo it. A retainer does not fix a missing system. It needs the system first, and then a named way to reach the people who remember why the page is shaped that way.

faqs.question: What should be in place on the day of launch?
faqs.answer: The client should hold the repository, the domain, the content logins, and a place where brand files and notes live. Staging should still be reachable for a short window. The sentences that explain the offer, and the list of what was refused, should be written down. Without those, the next edit starts from a screenshot.

faqs.question: Is a retainer the same as the second project?
faqs.answer: A retainer is a way to keep the same people available for a defined kind of change. The second project might be a larger slice, such as a new product area, and it can be scoped on its own. Either one fails if the first launch left no map. Either one can work if the map exists and the client can still reach the studio that drew it.

markdown:
A retainer after website launch survives only when the handoff left a system and a way to reach the same team. The second project dies, quietly, when the last delivery is a zip file and the people who knew the decisions have already moved on.

The client does not experience this as a strategy failure. They experience it as a site they are afraid to touch. The next studio, or the next hire, starts over because starting over is cheaper than archaeology.

## The second project starts at the handoff

Launch day is when the relationship either becomes a continuation or becomes a memory. If the client can change a headline, find the logo, and see why the homepage is structured as it is, they will come back with the next real problem. If they cannot, they will wait until the pain is large enough to justify a new agency, and the new agency will propose a rebuild.

Write the handoff as a set of objects, not a feeling of completion.

- The repository, in their account.
- The domain and the hosting, in their name.
- Content logins, with a note on what is safe to edit.
- Brand files: logo, type, colors, in a place that is not a chat attachment.
- A short decision log: the offer, the audience, what you refused.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone can tell who is responsible for a site and whether the content has a maintained purpose. A launch that scatters those facts fails the test in practice. The site may look finished. The client cannot keep it true. That is the gap the second project falls into.

On a Hanabi project the client portal is one concrete version of the place: brand files, docs, and updates after delivery. The tool can differ. The job cannot. If the only record is the designer's memory, the record leaves when they do.

## A system the next edit can use

The system does not have to be a vast kit. It has to be the decisions that stop a new page from inventing a second brand. Type sizes you actually use. The color that means action. The words for the primary objects. A component or two that the next landing page should reuse. Written where an engineer will open them, not only in a PDF.

Code is part of the system. A marketing site in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind can be continued by someone who was not in the original room, if the patterns are ordinary and the README says how to change a page. Clever one-off layouts, with the offer baked into an image, cannot. Leave the offer as text. Leave the layout as something a later person can extend without a fight.

Performance and motion belong in the note too. What you watched, and the reduced-motion behavior. A later editor who adds a hero video "for energy" will undo the launch if nobody wrote down why the page was quiet. The note can be half a page. Half a page beats a zip named Final_v7.

Figma, if you used it, should be in an account the client can open. A file trapped in a studio team becomes unreachable the month the subscription lapses, which is often the month they want a change. Export what must be exported. Share what must be shared. Say so in the handoff list, and check the link from their login, not from yours.

## The people who knew, and a way back

A system without a person still stalls, because the next question is judgment. "Can we add a second audience to the homepage?" The files will not answer. Someone who remembers the refusal will. If that someone is gone, and there is no path back, the client will ask a cheaper stranger, and the stranger will say yes.

Leave a named path. An email that a human reads. A call you can book. A retainer, if you both want a standing rhythm. The path should name who answers, and what kind of request fits. A small edit. A new page in the same system. A larger slice that needs its own proposal. Three doors, labeled, beat a vague "let us know if you need anything."

Introduce the person if the original lead will not be the one who stays. Do it before launch, on a real review, not in a footer of the invoice. The client should have heard the new person's judgment once, so the second project does not feel like a transfer to a stranger. If you cannot offer that continuity, say so. A clean ending is better than a retainer that is only a logo on a slide.

Same-day replies can be part of the path for questions. They are not a promise to design overnight. Write the difference down. Clients remember the promise they hoped for. You should have written the one you meant.

## What the retainer is for

A retainer is not a discount on undefined friendship. It is a reserved capacity for a kind of change you have both described. A set of hours, or a set of outcomes: one new page a month, a standing review, the edits that keep the offer true. Unused vagueness becomes resentment on both sides. The client feels they are paying for silence. The studio feels they are on call for surprises.

Define the intake. One channel. A short note on the job, the page, and the date they care about. The studio says whether it fits the retainer or needs a proposal. That sorting is the service. Without it, every message feels like it might be in scope, and the relationship becomes a queue of anxiety.

Review the retainer on a rhythm you choose in advance. Monthly is enough for many sites. Look at what changed, what hurt, and whether the system still holds. End or resize when the work has become a different shape. A retainer that quietly turned into a second full project, without a new slice, will blow up in the invoice. Name the new slice while it is still small.

Keep the public site's purpose stable while you do this. New pages should sound like the decision log. A retainer that publishes a different voice every month is not care. It is drift, billed monthly. The client portal, or whatever holds the notes, should get the decision each time, so month four does not depend on month one's memory.

## What kills it even with a contract

A contract does not survive a handoff the client cannot use. If they are locked out of the repository, the retainer is a dependency, and dependencies get replaced when budgets tighten. Ownership was the trust. Take it back, even gently, and the second project is already leaving.

Silence kills it. A launch followed by nothing, until they have a crisis, trains them to associate you with absence. A small scheduled note, even when little changed, keeps the path warm. You do not need news. You need to be findable. The status of the relationship should not be a mystery.

A new stakeholder kills it when they arrive to a site with no explanation. They will commission a rebrand to understand a decision that was never written down. The decision log is how you welcome them without starting over. Offer a short walkthrough. Do not mock the question. They were not in the room, and the room is over.

Cheap adjacent work kills it too. A founder asks for a "quick" landing page from a template shop because the retainer felt slow to invoke. The page launches off-system. Now there are two brands. The next request is to reconcile them, which is a worse project than the one you could have done in the system. Make the retainer easy to start, so the easy path is the consistent one.

## A clean ending when that is the truth

Not every launch should become a retainer. Some clients wanted a site and have the team to run it. Forcing a monthly fee is how you become the vendor they resent. Hand off the system, offer a way to return for a defined slice, and leave. The second project, if it comes, will come because the first one was usable without you.

Say this in the proposal, before the emotion of launch. "We can end at launch with a full handoff, or continue on a retainer shaped like this." Two honest options. The client chooses. You do not slide from one to the other in the final invoice.

If you end, schedule the last hour for questions while the work is fresh. Record the answers in the decision log. Remove your own access when they confirm they can publish, or leave access only as they ask. Lingering god-rights feel like help and read as risk. The handoff is complete when they can fire you and the site still runs.

Price the return, in outline, so a later email is not a cold start. "A new page in this system is a small project. A new product area is a proposal." They can budget. You can recognize the email when it arrives. Recognition is the opposite of the zip-file ending, where every future request feels like a stranger describing your own work back to you.

When the site and the product need a voice that a technical buyer will trust, the next problem is language. [Brand voice for a technical product](/blog/brand-voice-for-a-technical-product) is about writing the way a careful engineer explains a tool. Read it if the second project is a product surface and the launch voice will not survive a skeptical reader.
